text: Ines stood at the stove stirring a pot of lentils she would not eat. She had cooked for two for eleven years, and her hands still measured out two portions before she caught them. The kitchen was too quiet; the radio had been his, and she could not bring herself to switch it on. Steam rose and fogged the window. She thought about the weeks ahead, each one a copy of this evening, and could not find a single thing in them worth walking toward. Her shoulders felt like wet sand. When the lentils burned at the bottom, she simply turned off the flame and sat down on the floor.

Bram opened the fridge and looked at the shelves for a long time without seeing them. He had meant to make soup, the kind his mother used to make, but the recipe card in her handwriting sat on the counter and his chest folded in on itself each time he glanced at it. He peeled one carrot, then stopped. What was the point of a pot of soup for nobody. The knife felt heavy, the light felt grey, and the whole evening stretched out flat and empty. He put the carrot back, closed the fridge, and went to lie down with his coat still on.

Every morning Dara took the same train, and every morning the same fields slid past the window, brown and waterlogged. Today she did not open her book. She sat with her forehead against the cold glass and let the stations go by. The job waiting at the end of the line had stopped meaning anything months ago, and nothing else was waiting anywhere. Her body felt hollowed out, as if someone had scooped the middle out of her. A man across the aisle laughed into his phone, and the sound came from very far away. She thought, dully, that she could ride past her stop and it would not matter to anyone.

Oren missed the first bus and did not run for the second. He stood at the shelter while the rain came sideways, his hands in his pockets, his feet soaked through. Since the bakery closed he had been going to interviews that all ended the same way, and today's would too; he could already hear the polite voice. His throat was tight and his eyes stung. The street looked washed of color, like an old photograph of a place nobody lived in anymore. When the bus finally came, he watched its doors open and close and could not find the strength to lift his foot onto the step.

The phone rang at seven, as it did every Sunday, and Una let it ring out. It would be her sister, asking brightly whether she had been eating, whether she had gone outside. She had not. The curtains had been closed for four days. Una lay on the sofa and listened to the silence after the last ring, heavy as a blanket of stones. There was nothing she could say that would not bring them driving over, and nothing true that she could say at all. She thought of the years ahead as a long corridor with no doors in it, and she closed her eyes.

Kai's father called to say the farm had been sold. He said it plainly, the way he said everything, and then asked about the weather. Kai answered in single words. After the call he sat on the edge of the bed with the phone still warm in his hand. The orchard, the barn with the broken swing, the kitchen where his mother had lived her whole life: all of it gone to strangers now, and her with it, in a way. His chest ached with a dull, bottomless weight. He did not turn on the lamp when the room grew dark. There did not seem to be any reason to.

Esme had spent three months on the report, and on Monday the director cancelled the project in a two-line email. Nobody would ever read it. She scrolled through the pages anyway, the charts she had rebuilt at midnight, the notes in the margins. Her eyes went blurry and she let them. Around her the office hummed on, phones and keyboards, and she felt sealed off from all of it behind thick glass. Whatever she made next would end the same way, she thought; it always did. She saved the file in a folder she would never open again, and sat very still until everyone had gone home.

Gus had been at the warehouse for nineteen years when they told him the machines would take over his line by spring. He nodded, signed the paper, and went back to stacking boxes because there was nothing else to do with his hands. Each box felt heavier than the last. At fifty-eight, who would take him on. He pictured the empty days, the television on at noon, his wife pretending it was fine. His stomach sank and kept sinking. At lunch he sat in the car with his sandwich unopened on the seat beside him and stared at the grey wall of the loading bay.

The frost came early and killed everything in Pia's garden in a single night. She walked out in her slippers and found the beans black and limp, the tomatoes split, the marigolds collapsed onto the soil like wet paper. It had been the one thing she had kept going all year, the one reason to get up. She knelt down on the cold ground and did not get up for a long time. Her knees went numb. She thought that she could plant again in spring, and then thought that spring was very far away and she was very tired, and that nothing she tended ever lasted.

Lior had planted the apple tree the week his son was born. Now the tree was dying, its leaves curled and brown in July, and the man from the nursery had shaken his head. Lior stood beside it at dusk with a watering can he knew was useless. His son had not called in two years. The tree had been the last thing that still connected them, a silly thing, a tree. He pressed his palm against the rough bark and felt the old ache rise up through his arm and settle in his throat. The garden around him looked like a place that had already been abandoned.

The doctor spoke gently, which was how Vera knew. She heard words like manage and comfort and months, and the room seemed to tilt and then go very still. On the wall a poster showed a smiling family on a beach. Vera looked at it and thought of all the summers she had put off, all the trips she had meant to take next year. There would be no next year worth the name. Her hands lay in her lap like things that belonged to someone else. When the doctor asked if she had questions, she shook her head, because every question led to the same closed door.

Femi sat in the clinic corridor waiting for the results about his mother, though he already knew. The nurse's face had told him an hour ago. The plastic chair was hard and the vending machine buzzed. He kept thinking of her voice on the phone last Tuesday, how tired it had sounded, how he had promised to visit on the weekend. Now the weekend was here and she would not know him. His whole body felt weighed down, as if his bones had filled with lead. He watched the clock above the door and understood that nothing he did now could change anything at all.

The parcel was addressed to Rhea's brother, and it had come three weeks too late. Inside were the running shoes he had ordered, bright orange, size eleven, still wrapped in tissue. She held one of them in both hands on the doorstep. He had been training for the marathon in October. Now the shoes would sit in a cupboard, and October would come and go, and he would not be in it. Her legs gave way and she sat down hard on the step. The street carried on around her, a dog barking, a car door slamming, while she stayed there holding the shoe.

Another rejection letter arrived on Thursday, the forty-first. Milo did not need to open it to know; the envelope was thin. He had stopped keeping count out loud months ago, but the number lived in his chest like a stone. He laid the letter on the pile by the door with the others. Ten years of writing, and not one yes. He thought about the manuscript on his desk and could no longer remember why he had believed in it. His eyes burned. He went to the window and watched the postman walk on down the street, whistling, toward other houses and better news.

The dog's bowl was still by the back door, and Zola could not bring herself to move it. For fourteen years it had been there, and for fourteen years the old dog had waited by it at six o'clock sharp. Now it was six o'clock and the kitchen was silent. Zola sat at the table with her tea going cold. The lead hung on its hook. She kept expecting the click of claws on the floor, and each time the quiet came back instead, heavier than before. She pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes and stayed like that until it grew dark.

Nell's cat had not come home for nine days. She had put up posters on every lamp post, walked the streets calling at night, left food on the step that the foxes took. This morning the posters had faded in the rain and she did not print new ones. She sat on the back step with the empty food dish at her feet. The garden was grey. She understood, in a slow and final way, that the cat was not coming back, and the knowledge settled over her like a heavy wet coat she could not take off. Her chest ached every time she breathed in.

The new flat was smaller than Tavi had thought, and colder. She set the last box down in the middle of the bare floor and looked around at the damp corner, the single window facing a brick wall. This was what was left after the divorce: a kettle, some books, two chairs. She sat on one of the chairs and did not unpack. There did not seem to be any version of the future in which this room became home. Her arms hung limp at her sides. Outside a neighbor dragged a bin across the yard, and the scrape went on and on.

Jun taped up the last box in the house where he had grown up. His parents were both gone now, and the house had been sold to a young couple who would tear out the old kitchen. He walked through the empty rooms one last time. The marks on the doorframe where his mother had measured his height every birthday were still there. He touched them with one finger. His throat closed. Tomorrow the marks would be painted over and there would be nowhere left in the world that remembered him as a child. He locked the door and sat in the car without starting it.

Wren rode her bicycle along the canal path because the doctor had told her to get exercise, and because staying in bed had stopped working. The water was brown and still. Her legs pushed the pedals without any strength behind them, and every small hill felt like a mountain. She used to ride this path with Suki, laughing, racing to the bridge. Suki had moved abroad in spring and had stopped writing. Wren stopped at the bridge and leaned on the rail, breathing hard, and looked down at the flat water, and felt nothing move in her at all.

Amir's bicycle was stolen from outside the library on the one morning he forgot the lock. It was the bicycle his late wife had bought him for his sixtieth birthday. He stood staring at the empty rack, the cut cable on the ground. People stepped around him. It was only a bicycle, he told himself, and the telling did nothing. His knees felt weak and he sat on the library steps. It seemed to him that the world was taking her away piece by piece, and that soon there would be nothing left of her at all, and then nothing left of him.

Hana went to the market out of habit, with the canvas bag her husband used to carry. She stood at the fruit stall and could not remember what she had come for. The seller asked twice. Around her people bargained and joked, and the colors of the stalls seemed too bright, almost cruel. She bought three pears she did not want, because she had always bought three pears, one for each of them and one to share. The bag hung from her hand almost empty. Walking home, she felt every step drag, as if the pavement were pulling her down.

The stall had been in Teo's family for three generations, and today was its last Saturday. The rent had gone up again and the customers had gone to the supermarket. He set out the last crates of onions and potatoes the way his grandfather had taught him, in neat rows. Nobody came for an hour. He sat on an upturned crate with his head in his hands. By evening he would fold the awning for good, and the corner would become a car park. He could not picture what he would do with his mornings. Everything ahead of him looked grey and flat and empty.

Rain had been falling since dawn, and Cleo had not left the armchair. The house was dark because she had not turned on any lights. On the table sat the letter from the university saying her funding was cut and the lab would close. Eight years of her life had gone into that work. She watched the drops run down the window and join and fall. Her limbs felt too heavy to lift, and her thoughts moved slowly and always toward the same dead end. When the phone buzzed she turned it face down. The afternoon slid into evening and she stayed exactly where she was.

Zeb spent the rainy afternoon sorting through his father's things. The boxes smelled of pipe smoke and old paper. He found a birthday card he had sent at seven, kept all these years, and a photograph of the two of them fishing that he did not remember being taken. Outside, the gutters overflowed. He sat on the floor among the boxes with the card in his lap and his shoulders shaking. It had taken him too long to come home, and now there was no one to come home to. The rain went on and on, and the room grew dim around him.

Noor's oldest friend came for dinner and talked about her new job, her new house, her wedding plans. Noor smiled and nodded and passed the salad. Inside she felt a spreading hollowness. Her own year had been a long slide: the lost job, the breakup, the months in bed. She could not think of a single piece of news to offer. When her friend asked how she was, she said fine, and the word sat in her mouth like ash. After the door closed she stood in the hallway and felt the whole weight of the empty flat pressing in on her.

Quin had set the table for four, but only one friend came, and she left early. The others had sent short messages at the last minute. Quin cleared away the untouched plates and scraped the food into the bin. He had spent all day cooking. The candles burned down in the quiet room. He thought about how the invitations he sent had become rarer and the replies slower, how everyone had drifted into lives that had no room for him. His chest felt hollow and cold. He blew out the candles and sat in the dark among the smell of smoke.

The mechanic wiped his hands and said the car was not worth fixing. Ivo nodded. It was his grandfather's car, forty years old, and he had driven it to every important day of his life. Now it would be crushed into a cube at the scrapyard. He sat in the driver's seat one last time, his hands on the cracked wheel, the smell of old leather around him. Everything that mattered to him seemed to end like this, one by one, with a quiet verdict from someone who did not know what it meant. He could not make himself open the door and get out.

Sami's car broke down on the ring road in the rain, the third time this month. He did not have the money to fix it again, and without the car he could not get to the night shifts. He sat with the hazard lights clicking and watched the traffic spray past. His phone battery was at four percent. He thought of the rent, the overdue bills in the drawer, his daughter's shoes with the hole in them. There was no way out that he could see, only more of the same, stretching on. He rested his forehead on the steering wheel and closed his eyes.

Bea waited at the school gate as the other parents chatted in small groups. Her son came out last, alone, his head down, and she knew from his walk that it had happened again. Nobody had sat with him at lunch. He did not want to talk. They walked home in silence, his small hand limp in hers. She thought of all the schools they had tried and all the promises that things would get better. At home he went straight to his room. Bea stood in the hallway outside his door, her whole body heavy, unable to think of one thing that would help.

Every afternoon Rafa waited outside the school for his daughter, and every afternoon she came out and ran to her mother's car instead. Since the custody hearing he got two hours on Wednesdays, supervised. Today was not Wednesday. He stood across the road under a tree where she would not see him, just to watch her come out. She was laughing with a friend. Then the car door shut and she was gone. Rafa stayed under the tree long after the playground emptied, his hands in his pockets, feeling the weeks until Wednesday like an ocean he could not cross.

Suki swam out into the grey lake alone, as she and her mother used to do every summer. The water was cold and bit at her skin. Halfway to the buoy she stopped and floated on her back, looking up at the low clouds. Her mother's ashes had been scattered here in June. Suki let the water hold her. She thought that nothing she did now would ever be seen by the one person who had always watched. Her arms drifted out at her sides. The shore looked very far away, and for a long while she could not find the strength to swim back toward it.

Eli walked down to the beach at dawn, to the spot where he had once proposed. The tide was out and the sand was flat and grey for a mile. He took off his shoes and walked to the edge of the water, which was cold enough to make his ankles ache. The ring was in his pocket; she had given it back a week ago. He turned it over and over. Gulls wheeled over the mudflats. Everything he had planned for the next forty years had gone out with that tide, and there was nothing to replace it. He stood there until the water reached his shins, and did not move.
